chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Salih ibn al-Sindi, from Ja'far ibn Bashir, from Sabbah al-Hadda', from Abu Usama who said:
I accompanied Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him). He said to me: 'Read.' So I opened a Chapter from the Quran and recited it. He became soft-hearted and wept.

Then he said: 'O Abu Usama! Nurture your hearts by the Mention of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and be cautious of the instigation (nakat), for it comes upon the heart once or for many hours.' Doubt is from Sabbah. It is neither in it belief nor disbelief, like a worn-out piece of cloth or a decayed bone.

'O Abu Usama! Is it not that sometimes you inspect your heart, so you neither remember any good nor any evil by it, and nor do you know where it is?' I said to him, 'Yes, it has happened to me, and I have seen it happen to the people.' He said: 'Yes, everyone is exposed to it.'

So if it is like that, remember Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and be cautious of the instigation, for if He intends good for a servant, He instigates belief, and if He intends by it other than that, He instigates other than that.
I said, 'What is other than that, may I be sacrificed for you, what is it?' He said: 'If He intends infidelity, He instigates infidelity.'

key_terms.النَّكْتَ: Instigation or whispering (from the devil) that affects the heart's state
key_terms.الْخِرْقَةِ الْبَالِيَةِ: A worn-out piece of cloth (metaphor for the heart's state)
key_terms.الْعَظْمِ النَّخِرِ: A decayed bone (metaphor for the heart's state)

ai.seo_question: What is the meaning of 'nakat' (instigation) in the heart and how does one protect against it?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) advises Abu Usama to guard the heart against *al-nakat* (spiritual vacillation or whispering), describing it as a state of ambiguity where the heart is neither firmly in faith nor disbelief, akin to a worn cloth. This condition is universal to all humans, and divine will determines whether this state leads to faith or infidelity, emphasizing the need for constant *dhikr* to stabilize the heart. The narration highlights the Shia theological concept of the heart's susceptibility to spiritual fluctuation and the necessity of active remembrance to maintain spiritual clarity.
